Ta, Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an, and of a Book that makes things clear. (1)

The disjointed letters (huruf muqatta'at) actually draw attention to the fact that this Surah consists of the same material from which these letters are formed. Here, "Book" (kitab) refers to the Qur'an itself. The Qur'an is described as a "Book" (a written letter) for this reason: so that a comparison may be drawn between this Book and the reaction of the Quraysh to it, and between the letter of Solomon (Sulayman, peace be upon him) and the reaction of the Queen of Sheba (Saba) to it, even though Solomon (peace be upon him) was one of the servants of Allah.

After this introduction and challenge, the mention and description of the noble Qur'an proceeds as follows.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 27, verse 2:

﴿Hudan wa bushra lil-mu'minin﴾ (2)

This style is more eloquent than if it had been said, "In it there is guidance and good news for those who believe." The style adopted by the Qur'an conveys the meaning that the very content of this Book is itself guidance and good news. In this way, the Holy Qur'an guides the believers in every rise and fall of their lives. It is guidance from every aspect, and this Book is good news and glad tidings for the worldly and the otherworldly life of a person.

Is this Book guidance and good news only for the believers? In this phrase, Allah has packed a great and profound truth. This Qur'an is not a merely theoretical and philosophical book, such that whoever reads it, applies its subjects and implements them, and thereby the purpose of the Qur'an is fulfilled. This Book first addresses the heart and vision of a person so that he may accept it with faith, reverence and certainty. He should accept it with an open heart. Then this Book places its light, its awe and its wisdom into his heart, and to the extent that the reader's heart holds the freshness of faith, to that extent will he taste its sweetness. Its meanings will unfold before him, and its insights and interpretations will become clear to him. The secrets of this Book are not revealed to a hard-hearted person whose heart and mind are dry. Likewise, a sincere believer receives from it those guidance that the denier of truth and the hard-hearted do not receive, and by its light only the one who is a believer is guided, while the one whose heart and mind have been distorted does not find it.

Sometimes it happens that a person reads a certain verse or surah again and again. He passes over it in heedlessness and haste, and nothing settles in him. Suddenly a flash of light arises in his heart; worlds of meaning illuminate his mind, of which he had never even thought before. Thus, in such moments of illumination, a revolution comes into his life. He adopts one method and path in place of another.

In short, the system, law and morals taught in the Qur'an depend upon faith. Therefore, the person who has no faith in his heart, who does not regard this Holy Qur'an as revelation from Allah, and who does not believe that what has come in it is a system that Allah wishes to establish, such a person who does not have such faith and certainty about the Qur'an cannot obtain any guidance from the Holy Qur'an. For him there is then no good news in it, and no benefit.

The truth is that within the Holy Qur'an lie great treasures of guidance, knowledge, motivation and direction, but the key to opening the doors of these treasures is faith. These treasures cannot be opened without this key. Through the Qur'an, for those who truly embrace faith, such great feats emerge at their hands as are like the miracles of the prophets. But if the status of the Qur'an becomes that it is sung with melody, then in that case the Qur'an only strikes the eardrums and does not descend into the hearts. In that case the Qur'an brings no transformation, and no one benefits from it, and its status becomes like that of a treasure without a key.

In this Surah, the believers are also praised, those in whose hands is the key to reaching the treasures of the Qur'an; such people are like this.

He establishes the prayer and performs it in the manner its due right requires: when they stand before Allah, their hearts are awake, and at that moment they have the awareness that they are standing in the court of the Lord of Majesty and Honour. At that time their attention is fixed on that lofty horizon; their hearts are occupied with intimate communion with God, calling upon Him and present in His mighty court.

They give zakat, so that their souls are freed from the baseness of miserliness. Thus their spirits rise above the temptations of wealth, and they become connected with those needy brethren, delivering sustenance to them, and in this way discharge their collective responsibilities.

They hold firm conviction in the Hereafter. At all times they feel that they must answer before Allah in the Hereafter. Their hearts are occupied with matters of the Hereafter, their hearts are filled with the fear of God, and human desires do not affect their hearts. The fear of Allah and the grief of the reckoning of the Day of Judgment are consuming them.

These are the believers, those who remember Allah, those who fulfil His obligations, those who fear Him, the people of God-consciousness, hoping for His mercy and reward. These are the people whose hearts open up to the Qur'an, and for such people the Qur'an becomes guidance and glad tidings. It becomes the light of their souls; it warms their blood and makes their lives dynamic, and this Qur'an then becomes their provision for the journey, by means of which they reach the destination and become connected with their Lord.

Emphasizing further the remembrance of the Hereafter, it is said that those who do not have firm conviction in the Hereafter keep advancing in their misguidance, until suddenly they reach their end.

The fact is that faith in the Hereafter is the force that restrains human desires and emotions in this world and gives them moderation and balance. A person without faith has neither the power nor the moral strength to suppress any desire or inclination. Such a person thinks: "Be merry and indulge yourself, for this world does not come again, and life in this world is short." It is impossible that, if we forgo some pleasure or luxury in this world, or fail to obtain it, our life will be extended by even a moment. When this is the way of thinking, who can free a person from the grip of luxury, indulgence, and pleasures and desires, unless he develops within himself the belief that he will stand before Allah? He must hope for the reward and recompense of the Day of Judgment and fear the punishment of the Hereafter, the Day on which all people will stand.

Therefore, for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, every kind of lust and pleasure is made to appear attractive. Without fear of God, without fear of the Hereafter, and without shame, they run after these things like dogs. The nature and created disposition of the soul is inclined to pleasure; it is devoted to beauty and dies for what is beautiful. Unless it receives the guidance of the Signs of Allah and of the Noble Messenger, and they bring it within the sphere of faith, and it comes to understand that this world is transient. When a soul reaches this point, the colour of its deeds changes, and its state of longing changes. Then it finds delight in good deeds in the same way that it finds delight in material pleasures; indeed, the pleasure of the stomach and the body then appears to it as extremely base and trivial.

It is Allah who created man in this way. He has made him capable of this: if his heart opens to guidance, he can follow the path of guidance; and if his heart grows dim and the lamp of faith is extinguished, then he rushes headlong on the path of error. Moreover, for this guidance and misguidance of humanity, He has established a sunnah (established way), and according to it, a person either attains guidance or chooses the path of error. This is why the Qur'an makes it clear, and God declares it as His own act, that those who do not believe in the Hereafter:

﴿We have made their deeds appear fair to them, so they wander blindly﴾ (82 : 3). Because they do not believe in the Hereafter, the sunnah of Allah is enforced upon them, and thus their deeds, their pleasures and their desires are made attractive to them. Here, the meaning of "tazyin-e-a'mal" (making deeds appear fair), that is, making deeds seem adorned, is that they wander in such a way that they do not recognise the evil in which they are involved. Therefore they remain busy day and night in the cycle of evil, yet they have no awareness of it at all.

And for the one for whom evil has been made to appear attractive, his end is known to all.

Those are the ones for whom is a terrible punishment, and in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers. (27:5)

Whether this painful punishment reaches them in this world or in the Hereafter, the complete loss is the loss of the Hereafter. It corresponds exactly to people's deeds: the more a person inclines towards evil, the harsher the punishment there will be.

Now the introduction of this surah concludes with the point that, O Prophet, the source from which you are receiving the Qur'an is indeed the fountain of the Forbearing and the All-Wise.

"Tilqa" (you are receiving) in this word there is an indication that you are being given direct guidance from the All-Knowing, All-Wise Being, and this Being is one who makes everything in a wise manner and manages every matter with knowledge. The Qur'an is an example of this Being's knowledge and wisdom: in its method, in its commands and obligations, in its instructions and way of working, in the descent of its verses and commandments, and in the continuity of its parts and the balance and harmony of its subjects and themes.

Now the Qur'an takes up the stories (qisas), and from these stories it becomes known how effective Allah's wisdom and His extremely hidden plans are in this universe and in this Qur'an.

When Musa (peace be upon him) was returning from Madyan towards Egypt, his wife, and the daughter of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), were also his companions. On a dark, cold night, he lost his way. His words were: "I shall bring you either some news from there, or a firebrand so that you may warm yourselves." At that time Musa was on one side of Mount Tur. And in that era it was the custom to light fires on high mounds at night, so that if a traveller lost his way he might be guided. In such a case, when a traveller came, he would receive hospitality, could warm himself against the cold, and would also be shown the way through the desert.

﴿Inni anastu nara﴾ (20:10): "I have perceived a fire." When he saw the fire from afar, he gained a measure of reassurance, and hope arose that by going to that fire he would receive some guidance, or would bring back a firebrand with which he could kindle a fire and warm himself in that desert.

Musa (peace be upon him) advanced towards the fire he had seen, so that he might bring back some news from there. Suddenly there, he hears a most dignified and majestic voice.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah an-Naml (27), verses 8–9:

﴿Fa-lamma jaa'ha nudiya...al-Hakim﴾ (27:9)

This is the call with which the whole universe moves in step, and with which all worlds and all heavens are in harmony. The entire creation stands awestruck before it, and the human soul and conscience tremble on hearing it. It is the voice through which earth and heaven are joined, and through which a small speck of a human being hears the voice of the Great and Exalted Being, and a mortal, weak human is bound to the immortal, mighty Being of the Lord. And this station is granted to him only through the grace of the Lord, may He be exalted.

﴿Fa-lamma jaa'ha nudiya﴾ (27:8): "When he came to it, he was called." The Qur'an does not name the one calling, yet he is known. This omission and the use of the passive form are for reverence, magnification and the majesty of the Greatness of Allah.

﴿Nudiya an buurika man fi-n-nari wa man hawlaha﴾ (27:8): "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it." Who was in the fire, and who was around the fire? The preferred interpretation is that this was not an ordinary fire such as we kindle, but a fire whose source was the higher realm. It was a fire which the pure angels had lit for a great guidance, and it appeared like fire, and within it were pure souls. Therefore the call, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire," was an announcement that those in this fire and those around it who are pure souls are blessed. And around this fire was Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) as well. The whole universe recorded this honour: that this patch of earth is a blessed place in the whole universe, a sacred site, upon which the manifestations and blessings of Allah, the Lord of Majesty, have descended; and then the sanctity and blessing of this place were also proclaimed. Besides this, it was also recorded: "Glory be to Allah, Lord of all the worlds. O Musa! Indeed, I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise."

﴿Wa subhana Allahi Rabbi-l-'alamin﴾ (27:8) ﴿Ya Musa innahu ana Allahu-l-'Aziz al-Hakim﴾ (27:9): In this verse, Allah announced the purity of His Being and His lordship over the entire universe, and also made known that the voice coming is Mine, the Mighty, the Wise. Through the person of Musa (peace be upon him), the whole of humanity was granted this elevation, and he became a shining star in the sky of the universe. Musa (peace be upon him) received from near that fire a very great news which he had seen from afar, but this great news was also a great responsibility. He was given a burning ember that warms, but it was a fire leading the people to the path of guidance.

This call was to choose Musa (peace be upon him), to place upon him the duty of prophethood, and to convey the message to those who were the greatest rebels on this earth. Thus Allah prepares him for this task, trains him, and equips him with proofs and miracles.

The same thing happened here as well: Moses put his hand into his collar, and when he drew it out, it was shining without any illness. The remaining signs are not enumerated here, whereas the details are given in Surah al-A'raf, which are these: drought, shortage of produce, the storm, the locust swarm, lice, frogs and blood. Since the subject of Surah al-A'raf was that Moses, peace be upon him, was given mighty signs, yet Pharaoh still denied them, nevertheless, despite the signs being clear and sufficient, the people rejected them.

When their signs came to them, clear and plain, they said, "This is clear magic." (27:13)

These were countless signs, signs that clearly distinguish truth from falsehood, signs so evident that anyone whom Allah has given two eyes can see them. Allah describes them as ﴿mubsirah﴾, meaning they are things that give sight, guiding people to the path of right guidance as they look at them. Yet these people were so obstinate that they called them ﴿sihrun mubin﴾, clear magic. It was not that they truly said this from the heart, or that they actually believed it. They said it only out of injustice and arrogance. Their hearts and minds were in fact convinced that this was the truth. They had no doubt at all.

﴿And their souls were convinced of them, though they denied them out of injustice and arrogance.﴾ (27:14) They denied them purely out of stubbornness and obstinacy, because they did not want to believe, nor did they wish to seek any proof. They regarded themselves as superior to the truth, and in doing so they wronged themselves, for accepting the truth was itself their own benefit.

The same condition prevailed among the leaders of Quraysh. They heard the Qur'an, and they were well assured that it was the truth, yet they rejected it purely out of obstinacy. They denied the call of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that call was directed to Allah alone. The reason was that these people wanted to remain upon their religion and beliefs in every circumstance, because within that religion were principles through which they held positions of authority and enjoyed certain interests. These positions and interests were founded upon those false beliefs. The danger they saw in the Islamic call was that its success would end these interests, and their status and standing would be lost. They knew that the ground was slipping from beneath their feet, and that an earthquake was shaking their beliefs and their consciousness. The Qur'an was a clear truth, and its effective blows fell upon them constantly.

The denial of truth does not always occur because people do not know it. Rather, truth is denied because people know what its consequences will be. Their own souls know this well. Moreover, such deniers do not fear for their lives, but for their circumstances, their interests, and their advantages. Therefore they stand firmly against the truth, even though the truth is clear and manifest.

﴿Then see how was the end of the corrupters.﴾ (27:14) See what became of Pharaoh and his people. The Qur'an has given the full details of this in other places; here it has only alluded to it. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 27, verse 15:

Lesson No. 271: At a Glance

"Here there is only a single allusion to Dawud (ʿalayhi al-salām), but the whole story is that of Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām), and before it a brief link of the story of Musa (ʿalayhi al-salām) has been given. All these personalities were among the prophets of the Children of Israel, and at the very beginning of this surah, while commenting on the Qur'an, this was stated:

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an narrates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ﴾ (27:76)

In this surah, more details are given of the story of Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām) than in all the other surahs, that is, wherever Sulayman is mentioned. Although here, from his life events, the details of the Hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba are given. It begins thus: Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām) declares that Allah has especially taught him the speech of birds, has granted him everything, and he thanks Allah for the favour and grace He has bestowed upon him. After this, a scene appears in which Sulayman is seen marching with his hosts. In this great army are jinn, humans and birds, all included. When this army moves, a small ant warns its people that a mighty, thundering army is heading towards this area. Therefore, save yourselves. Sulayman hears these words and also thanks his Lord for this. Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām) realises that a blessing is also a trial. Therefore he prays: O Allah, grant me, in this trial, the ability to be grateful and to succeed.

Why has this story been brought in this surah? At the beginning of the surah it was stated that this is a Book of guidance, and then in the same surah it was said that this Qur'an narrates to the Children of Israel most of the matters about which they hold differing opinions, as we have already said earlier, and the stories of Musa, Dawud and Sulayman (ʿalayhim al-salām) are important links in the history of the Children of Israel.

The connection of the link of the story of Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām) presented here with the theme of this surah: this link has connection with the subject of this surah in several respects.

The central theme of this surah is knowledge, as we have said in the commentary on this surah. And in the story of Dawud and Sulayman, the very first allusion is towards this.

"This Qur'an narrates to the Children of Israel most of the matters about which they differ."

﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾ (27:15), "We gave knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman." And then in this link Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām), alluding to the knowledge of the speech of birds (manṭiq al-ṭayr), acknowledged the blessing of Allah:

﴿And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds"﴾ (27:16). And in the midst of this story, the Hoopoe, stating the reason for its absence, says:

﴿I have acquired knowledge of that which you have not encompassed; and I have come to you from Sheba with certain information﴾ (27:22). And then in this story it is said that the one who had knowledge of the Book said that he would bring the throne of the Queen of Sheba in the blink of an eye.

At the opening of the surah it was stated that this Qur'an is a clear Book from Allah and it has been sent for the guidance of the polytheists of Makkah. But they deny it. Then in it there is mention of a letter of Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām) that was written to the Queen of Sheba. But when she realises that Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām) calls to the truth, she and her people soon accept it and become obedient, especially when they see that the forces of jinn, humans and birds have also been subjected to Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām), and that it is Allah who has granted Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām) these powers. He is the Possessor of supreme sovereignty.

Then in this surah there is also mention of Allah's favours upon human beings. There is also mention of His signs in this universe. But the state of people is that even so they deny the signs of Allah and do not render the thanks due for blessings. In this story too there is mention of a grateful servant who raises his hands in supplication before Allah, saying: O Allah, grant me the ability to render due thanks for Your favours. Those who reflect upon the signs of Allah and never become heedless of them at any time, and who do not become insolent because of Allah's favours, nor are they afflicted with arrogance because of power. Therefore the theme of this story has many connections and correspondences with the surah, and in the subject of the surah and within the story there are clear indications everywhere.

The way the Qur'an has narrated the story of Sulayman and the Queen of Sheba is an example of how the Qur'an brings stories and what its artistic style of narrating stories is like. In this story there are effort and struggle, emotions and impressions, various scenes and sights, and then the gaps between various scenes in which unnecessary parts have been cut out. And there are its other artistic excellences.

Now, let us look at the details of the verses.

Lesson No. 271: Explanation of the Verses

51 to 44

﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman. And they said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ (27:15)

"(This is an indication that the story is about to begin, and these are introductory words. It is announced that We bestowed great blessings upon the major characters of this story, and the greatest honour was knowledge, which was given to Dawud and Sulayman (ʿalayhima al-salām). The knowledge given to Dawud is detailed in other surahs of the Qur'an. He was given the art of reciting the Psalms (Zabur) with proper cadence (tartil), and he was so skilled in this art that when he recited the verses of the Zabur, the whole of creation would hum along with him. The echo of the mountains and the chirping of birds would sing the Zabur along with him, because his voice was extremely sweet. He recited with heartfelt feeling and became absorbed in intimate supplication with his Lord. Then Allah had given him the basic technology of military equipment. He made good coats of mail, was skilled in melting metals, and made all kinds of things from them, and he was an excellent judge, and in this work Sulayman was his special adviser.

As for Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām), in this surah the full details are given of what Allah taught him, namely the speech of birds, and as mentioned in other surahs, that he was an excellent judge, and the winds were also subjected to him, and the story begins with this very allusion.

﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾ (27:15). "It is a fact that We gave knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman." But before the verse ends, from the very souls of Sulayman and Dawud (ʿalayhima al-salām) it comes forth that they render thanks to the Lord for this blessing, and that knowledge, as a blessing, is held in high esteem by them. In thanking Allah they say that Allah has preferred them in this matter over a large number of His believing servants. Thus they acknowledge the worth of knowledge and then the great favour.

Here the nature and details of that knowledge are not given, because absolute knowledge, in the sight of Allah, is a bounty from Him. The purpose is to show that knowledge in general is a blessing of Allah. Every kind and every type of knowledge is desired for the believer. Then it is the duty of every scholar to render thanks for this bounty of Allah, and to keep on declaring the praise and glory of Allah, and to keep on supplicating: O Allah, let this knowledge be beneficial to me. Such knowledge is not a cause of salvation, success and felicity for its possessor, nor can such knowledge be beneficial for people. Such knowledge becomes a cause of calamity, misfortune, fear, anguish, restlessness and ultimately destruction for humanity, because this knowledge has been cut off from its source and origin, its direction is wrong, and it has lost the path to reach Allah.

But the bitter fruit that humanity has picked and eaten at the hands of those who obtained this atomic knowledge and in whose hearts there was no fear of God. This is because in the hearts of these people there was no fear of God, no glorification of God, and no attention to God. Consequently this knowledge and such scientists carried out the deed of Hiroshima, caused the destruction of Nagasaki, and after these events, all people of East and West are waiting day and night for the destruction of this earth and of all humanity.

After this preface, that We gave knowledge to both Dawud and Sulayman, and they praised Allah that He had shown them favour and felt the worth of knowledge, now only the events of the life of Sulayman (ʿalayhi al-salām) are narrated."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 27, verse 16:

Dawud (David) (peace be upon him) was given prophethood and knowledge, and along with these, he was also given sovereignty. However, in the mention of Allah's grace and favour upon these two, his authority is not mentioned. Only knowledge and wisdom are mentioned, because in comparison to knowledge and wisdom, sovereignty is a lowly thing.

﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾ (27:16). Here, inheritance also refers to the inheritance of knowledge, because it is only knowledge and wisdom that is worthy of one prophet inheriting from another. This emphasis is also indicated by the fact that Sulayman (peace be upon him) announces among the people:

﴿"O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of everything."﴾ (27:16) So the knowledge is mentioned explicitly, and the remaining blessings are mentioned within its scope. As if to say: Dawud did not give these things; rather, the Giver is Allah, from whom knowledge came.

﴿"O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of everything."﴾ (27:16) Sulayman (peace be upon him) announces these matters among the people. He makes this announcement as a mention of Allah's blessing, and for the sake of his high status with Allah, not as boasting or self-glorification. It is not that he wished to overawe the people and spoke of things that were not in them. That is why the following is mentioned:

﴿"Indeed, this is manifest grace."﴾ (27:16) That is, it is Allah's grace upon His servant, because only Allah is capable of teaching the speech of birds, and in this way Dawud and Sulayman were given, in general, all kinds of favours. These too can only be given by Allah.

Allah has provided means for birds, animals and creeping creatures to make one another understand, and this is their language and logic. Allah is the Creator of all these worlds. He says:

﴿And there is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you﴾ (6:38). These can be communities only when there are collective ties among them, according to which they live, and there are means and mediums through which they understand one another. Such features are visible in countless insects, animals and birds. Experts in the various kinds of creeping creatures have, through their estimates and observations, discovered some signs of the means of communication of these species, though these are speculative. As for the knowledge that was given to Sulayman (peace be upon him), it was specific to him and was given to him in a miraculous manner; it was not the common observation of ordinary people, nor was it knowledge like that which some people in our age have learned about certain species through observation and investigation. These human sciences are conjecture and estimation. The nature of theirs and the nature of Sulayman's (peace be upon him) knowledge are different.

I wish to clarify this further for emphasis, because some modern commentators have been so impressed by the scientific achievements of science that they interpret the Qur'an in the light of modern scientific discoveries. These commentators have interpreted the knowledge of the speech of birds (Mantiq al-Tayr) of Sulayman (peace be upon him) in such a way that it was the same kind of knowledge as some modern experts have learned about creeping creatures and certain genera and species of animals. Such efforts actually strip Qur'anic miracles of their true reality. This is in fact a defeated way of thinking, and it bows unnecessarily before modern science. Whereas the discoveries of science are very insignificant and limited, while for Allah it is no difficult matter to make a person understand all the modes of expression and dialogue of animals, creeping creatures and birds and beasts, and to make him understand them in a miraculous manner. Without scientific research or effort, it is easy for Allah: the barrier He has placed between humans and animals only needs to be removed. He is the Creator of all kinds.

Furthermore, this was one aspect of the great miracle given to Sulayman (peace be upon him). Its second source was that a large number of jinn and birds were subjected to him, so that they would be under his government and fully obedient to him, just as the armies of men that he had enlisted, and the group of birds that was placed under his command, were given by Allah a special power of support, which such ordinary birds did not possess.

This is evident from the story of the hoopoe (hudhud), which investigated the affairs of the kingdom of the Queen of Sheba and understood her conditions in the manner that a highly intelligent and God-fearing person can understand. This too was part of the miracle given to Sulayman.

It is Allah's way (sunnah) that among the animals found in Allah's creation, the level of intelligence may be high or low, but no animal attains the status that its perceptive faculty surpasses or equals that of a human. This is not the divine sunnah in the creation of animals and birds. Nor is this sunnah in harmony with the system of this entire universe, nor does it follow the divine sunnah. This sunnah has been running in exactly this way since the very first day.

Today, the hoopoe found among us was being born in this same pattern thousands of millions of years ago. Since Allah created it, the hoopoe of today is an exact copy of the hoopoe created thousands of millions of years ago, because Allah has placed in every animal such genes that today's hoopoe is a complete copy of the hoopoe created thousands of millions of years ago. Whatever change occurs within it, it cannot go beyond the boundary of its own kind. This too is one aspect of the divine sunnah and is in harmony with this universe.

However, despite these two realities, these laws of nature and this divine sunnah do not prevent Allah from producing an exceptional case within the principles of His power. Sometimes this exceptional state is in fact a part of the general law and continuing sunnah, but we are not aware of this particular aspect. Knowledge of this partial law and exceptional state belongs in reality only to Allah. Allah suspends an apparently operating principle. Thus, the apparent change in the divine sunnah is also a higher sunnah. This was the story of the hoopoe and Sulayman, and Allah subjected those powers to Sulayman (peace be upon him).

Now we come from this point to the story of Sulayman (peace be upon him): what blessings he received from Allah after inheriting from Dawud.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 27, verse 17:

وحشر ……یوزعون (71)

This was the army of Hazrat Sulayman. It was gathered from every direction in a very large number, consisting of jinn, humans and birds. Humans are known. The jinn are a creation about which the Qur'an itself has given information, and regarding their reality the Qur'an says that they are created from a flame of fire, that is, flames that rise in the form of waves. Humans cannot see them, but they can see humans.

﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you cannot see them﴾. Although this verse is about Iblis, he was among the jinn. Then, these jinn have the power to cast evil whisperings into the hearts of humans, and then they incite humans to disobedience of Allah. But we do not know the detailed manner of this. Also, a group of jinn did believe in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not see them. Nor did he see or hear their belief. However, Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ of this matter.

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened, and said: "Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an, which guides to the path of right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord."﴾ (72:1-2) (28:1-2 in the source)

We know that a group of jinn was also subject to Hazrat Sulayman (peace be upon him), who made for him arches, images, and large basins like cooking vessels, and these jinn would dive into the sea for him and carry out his other commands, and all of them were present with his army alongside humans and birds.

And when we say that Allah subjected a group of jinn and humans to Hazrat Sulayman (peace be upon him), it is because not all the jinn and humans of the entire earth were part of Hazrat Sulayman's army, since the bounds of Hazrat Sulayman's kingdom were limited to Palestine, Syria and Iraq. Likewise, not all jinn and not all birds were subject to him. Only a group of them was subjected to him.

Not all the jinn were subjected, because Iblis was among the jinn, and his offspring were also jinn, as the Qur'an states: ﴿He was of the jinn﴾, and in Surah an-Nas it is stated that he casts whisperings into the hearts of people. In the time of Hazrat Sulayman too, the devil jinn would cast whisperings into the hearts of people, misguide them, and incite them to all evil deeds. Therefore, not all the jinn were subject to Hazrat Sulayman, for otherwise, being under his subjugation, how could they have done corrupt deeds? Because Hazrat Sulayman was a prophet who called people to guidance. Therefore the correct position is that a group of the jinn was under his command.

The same reasoning applies to the birds: when the hoopoe was not found, it became clear that not all birds were subjected to him, for otherwise the absence of one among thousands of birds would not have been noticed. When the hoopoe was not found, he said: ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe? Is he among the absent?﴾ (27:20). It became clear that this was a specific hoopoe. It may be that this was the only hoopoe, or that the hoopoe on duty was not present. It also shows that Allah had given this hoopoe, or the subjugated hoopoes, a somewhat greater power of perception which other hoopoes did not have, and this perceptive power was only for those birds that were subjected to Sulayman (peace be upon him). For from the hoopoe's speech in these verses it is evident that he was an intelligent and righteous bird.

In short, a great army of jinn, humans, wild beasts and birds was gathered for Hazrat Sulayman. It was a great army, and all of them were extremely well organized. It was not in the form of an unorganized crowd. Therefore they are called armies (afwaj), and the word junud conveys both meanings: multitude in number and organization.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (*Fi Zilal al-Quran*, Urdu translation) on Surah 27, verses 18–19:

﴿Until, when they came upon the Valley of the Ants……among Your righteous servants﴾ (91)

When this army set out, comprising humans, jinn and birds, its front was linked to its rear with perfect organisation and order. Its ranks were disciplined and its movement was orderly. This army reached a valley where ants were present in large numbers, so numerous that the valley itself was named Wadi an-Naml (the Valley of the Ants). Then an ant, who was their leader, said to the ants:

﴿Enter your dwellings﴾ (81–82) "Enter your dwellings." It is worth noting that ants, like honeybees, are highly organised. Duties are divided among them, and they live by a remarkable system, a system so orderly that it is difficult for humans themselves to live with such organisation. They have been given highly developed intelligence and a strong power of perception. Then that ant spoke in its own language:

﴿Let not Sulayman and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive﴾ (81–82) "Let not Sulayman and his armies crush you, while they are unaware." Sulayman understood the ant's words. His heart was greatly pleased that an ant was issuing commands. He was amazed that an ant knew the stature of Sulayman, and that it felt fear, while there was no intention in his heart to harm it, as a small creature fears the harm of a large one. Sulayman was pleased that so small a creature had awareness of him, and then he was also astonished that an ant's obedience was understood and carried out by him. He was greatly amazed at the creatures and wonders of Allah.

When Sulayman (peace be upon him) came to know all these matters:

﴿So he smiled, laughing at her words﴾ (82:91) "So Sulayman smiled and laughed at her words." However, this observation shook him and turned his heart towards the Lord, Who had granted him this knowledge beyond the ordinary. Thus the veils of mystery that lay between humans and other creatures were lifted. Accordingly, Sulayman (peace be upon him) turned to his Lord with great humility.

﴿And he said: My Lord, grant me inspiration that I may be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents﴾ (82:91) "He said: O my Lord, keep me under control so that I may continue to thank You for the blessing You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents."

O Lord, this is directly the supplication of a man who had attained nearness to God. *Awzi'ni* means: gather me together. Keep my consciousness and my limbs gathered; keep my heart and my tongue under control. Regulate my thoughts and my inner turmoil, and gather my words and my acts of worship. Regulate my deeds and my activities. Regulate all my powers and bring them together. Unite my faculties from beginning to end. All these meanings are included in *awzi'ni*, so that I may become a complete embodiment of gratitude for the favours bestowed upon me and upon my parents.

From this manner of expression it becomes clear that these favours had a profound effect on the heart of Sulayman (peace be upon him). The nature of that effect is also made manifest by it, and his existence and his inner sense were saturated with this rain of Allah's grace and kindness. He believed that Allah's gentle hand was constantly upon him and upon his parents, with blessing, mercy, and grace.

"O my Lord, keep me under control so that I may continue to thank You for Your favour which You bestowed upon me and upon my parents."

﴿And that I may do righteous deeds which please You﴾ (82:91) "And that I may do righteous deeds which please You." Righteous deeds are in reality also the grace of Allah, and they are bestowed upon the person who is grateful to Allah. Sulayman (peace be upon him) is so grateful that in this matter he seeks Allah's help, for gratitude itself is not possible without Allah's assistance, and the ability to act is also a blessing from Him. Sulayman (peace be upon him) had a good awareness of this point.

﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ (82:91) "And by Your mercy admit me among Your righteous servants." You know that to be among the servants of Allah and to join them is also Allah's mercy. Through it, a person is helped, and is granted the ability to do good deeds. Then he walks with the righteous, and supplicates to Allah that he may be among those upon whom Your mercy falls, who are travellers on Your path and are in that company. Sulayman humbles himself before Allah, although he is a prophet, and humans, jinn and birds are subjected to him, yet he still regards himself as in need of Allah's mercy. He fears that he might fall short in giving thanks for the blessing of righteous deeds. In short, this keen sense, this very awareness, this fear and reverence of Allah, and this firm consciousness of seeking His pleasure and mercy, are the moments in which Allah's blessings descend openly upon His special servants, as they descended upon Sulayman.

Here before us there are not one but two miracles. One miracle is that Sulayman (peace be upon him) came to know, and the other is that the ant came to know that this army belonged to Sulayman (peace be upon him). The first miracle is that Allah taught Sulayman. He was a prophet and a human being, and regarding a human, one can understand with ease that he came to know the ant's commands. But the second miracle, contained in the ant's words, can be explained by saying that the ants came to know that humans are a large creature who would trample them. Every living creature has within it the urge to preserve its life, and likewise ants have such awareness. As for how an ant came to know that this vast army of a large creature belonged to Sulayman (peace be upon him), this is nonetheless a miracle, and it should be regarded as a miracle, for Allah miraculously taught it this.

Now let us turn to the account of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and the Hoopoe, and his dealings with the Queen of Sheba. In this story there are six important scenes. There are gaps between these scenes. Unnecessary events have been omitted. The intervening events and scenes come to mind after one has seen the scenes. In this way, in narrating the story, there is a display of superior artistry, and between these scenes there are some instructive remarks in which human consciousness is drawn towards the purpose and goal for which this story has been brought. In this way the true purpose of bringing the story is fulfilled. Thus both aims are achieved: the beauty of artistic expression, and the moral lesson and religious teaching.

At the very beginning of speaking about Sulayman (peace be upon him), mention was made of humans, jinn and birds, and there was an indication of the blessing of knowledge among Allah's favours upon Sulayman (peace be upon him). Therefore, in this story the important role of humans, jinn and birds is present throughout, and the role of all of them is again connected with knowledge. The important roles were also alluded to in the introduction of this surah, and this is an important feature of Qur'anic narratives.

Furthermore, the characters in this story, their personalities, their distinguishing qualities and traits are also present in the narrative: the personality of Sulayman, the personality of the Queen of Sheba, the personality of the Hoopoe, the personalities of the courtiers of the Queen of Sheba, and the psychology, thinking and inclinations of these personalities and characters are all present in the story.

Sulayman (peace be upon him) hears the ant's speech, turns towards Allah, offers thanks, and supplicates: "O Allah, increase, increase."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 27, verses 20–21:

وتفقد……مبین (13)

In this scene, Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him) appears among his great and vast army. When he inspects the birds, he finds the hoopoe (Hudhud) missing. This shows that it was a particular hoopoe that ought to have been present in this army. It was not an ordinary hoopoe, such that one out of millions might be absent, or that it was merely one fewer among all the hoopoes of the earth. Furthermore, it also shows that this particular hoopoe had a distinct role and distinctive qualities. It was an extremely alert, observant and intelligent hoopoe. And the personality of Sulayman (peace be upon him) is also apparent: he keeps a full watch even over his great and mighty army, knowing the army from beginning to end.

He speaks about this in the precise and comprehensive words of a high commander-in-chief.

مالی لا اری الھدھد ام کان من الغآئبین (27 : 20) "What is the matter? I do not see the hoopoe. Or is he among the absentees?" It appears that the hoopoe is absent, and everyone knows that when the king asks about it, he is absent without permission. Therefore this matter is now taken seriously, so that there is no disorder within the army and others do not begin to slip away here and there. Because after the king's inquiry, the matter was no longer a secret. If this were not considered seriously, it would be a bad example for the other soldiers. Accordingly, Sulayman takes the absence of this soldier of his army very seriously.

لا عذبنہ عذاباً شدیداً اولا اذبحنہ (27 : 21) "I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will slaughter him." But nevertheless, he was a Prophet... not a tyrant. As yet he has not heard the hoopoe's excuses and has not been given notice, so the decision will be made after hearing his excuses. A decision made without hearing is contrary to the Islamic principle of justice. Therefore it is said:

ولیاتینی بسلطن مبین (27 : 21) "Or he must bring me a clear justification." That is, a proof and an excuse by which he may escape accountability, and the excuse must be reasonable.

Qutb, commentary on verses 27:29–31 (Urdu translation of *Fi Zilal al-Quran*)

﴿Qālat …… Muslimīn﴾ (27:29–31)

She tells her council that this letter has been thrown into her court. From this it appears that she did not know who had thrown it or how it had been thrown. If she had known that it was thrown by the hoopoe (hudhud), as some commentators have said, she would have announced it, because that would have been another strange matter. Hoopoes throwing letters were not an everyday miracle. Since she used the passive verb "ألقي" (ulqiya, "was thrown"), and since Allah has related it in this form, we understand that she did not know who had thrown the letter.

The queen calls it a noble letter, "Kitāb Karīm." Perhaps, from the style of its writing, its seal, and the manner of its delivery, she concluded that it was no ordinary letter. Moreover, when she informed her advisers of its contents, their reaction deepened her sense of the letter's importance. Its contents were as follows:

﴿Innahu min Sulaymān wa innahu bismillāhi al-Raḥmāni al-Raḥīm. Allā taʿlū ʿalayya wa atūnī muslimīn﴾ (27:30–31): "Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it begins: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Do not exalt yourselves against me, but come to me in submission."

She was not a Muslim, but the influence of Sulayman's (peace be upon him) rule was widespread in that region. The Qur'an's report of the letter's words shows that it was a direct letter, of very firm, awe-inspiring and frightening content. For this reason she called it a noble letter.

The content of the letter is very simple, and its opening, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," is extremely impactful. Its message is only this: do not rebel against me, and come before me in submission. Yet it is not submission before Sulayman himself, but before Allah: come as Muslims.

The queen placed this book and letter before her leading men, the people of "ahl al-ḥall wa al-ʿaqd" (literally, those who loose and bind, meaning the leading and decision-making notables), and sought their counsel on the matter. She said that she never decides any matter before consulting them. Everything is done with their consent and their unanimous agreement.

The content of the letter is very simple, and its opening, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," is extremely impactful. Its message is only this: do not rebel against me, and come before me in submission. Yet it is not submission before Sulayman himself, but before Allah: come as Muslims.

The queen placed this book and letter before her leading men, the people of "ahl al-ḥall wa al-ʿaqd" (literally, those who loose and bind, meaning the leading and decision-making notables), and sought their counsel on the matter. She said that she never decides any matter before consulting them. Everything is done with their consent and their unanimous agreement.

The passage is a commentary on the verse quoted in part here, so the Qur'anic quotation should be kept with its markers. The Qur'anic fragment "قالت ……تشھدون (23)" is the start of the verse (27:32): ﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me. Indeed, it is from Sulayman and indeed it says, 'In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful...' Do not be haughty toward me but come to me in submission." She said, "O chiefs, advise me in my affair; I have not been deciding a matter until you have been present."﴾

Here is the translation of the commentary:

This shows how extremely clever a woman the Queen of Sheba is. She took up this letter even though there is no trace of the one who threw it. From the letter it appears that it is decisive, and that the one who wrote it is some superpower. She conveyed this impression to the minds of her counsellors (ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd) in such a way that she called it an important, open and noble letter (kitab karim). This makes it clear that this queen does not want to confront, but she does not openly express this either. By way of preface she says it, then she asks for opinion, and the reply of her courtiers (hashiya-nashin) comes. As is their habit, they say: command us, we are ready. We are strong, but in any case the decision rests with Your Majesty!

**﴿They said: ... you command﴾ (23)**

Here the true character of this woman now comes into view. She is in the form of the Queen of Sheba. Every woman, by nature, dislikes destruction and ruin. Therefore she wishes to try the weapon of statecraft and planning before the weapon of military equipment.

She said: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it … and the messengers will return.﴾

She knows that when kings take control of a settlement, they lay it waste. (In Arabic, the word *qaryah* is also used for a large city.) They dishonour the people, shed blood, and utterly break the strength of the local population. They first eliminate the existing chiefs and influential classes, because it is these people who resist and defend. This is their historical pattern of conduct.

A gift softens the human heart and creates affection. Sometimes a modest gift averts a very great war. This is an established experience. If Prophet Sulayman accepts the gift, it will be a worldly affair, and in the world such means are effective and yield benefit. And if he does not accept it, it will be a matter of principle, and ideological movements cannot be stopped with money, nor can the tactics of this world stop them.

Now the curtain falls again. In the next scene, the agents of the Queen of Saba present the gifts before the court of Prophet Sulayman, and Prophet Sulayman disapproves of their conduct in wanting to purchase him with wealth and property, and in wanting to buy the Islamic call for a few trifling coins. Accordingly, Prophet Sulayman gives them a stern warning and issues a severe threat.

He said, ﴿...before your glance returns to you﴾.

Do you know for what purpose Sulayman (peace be upon him) had the throne brought before she submitted? The correct view is that Sulayman (peace be upon him) did this so that he could show the Queen of Saba that the miraculous powers of the universe were supporting him, so that the Queen of Saba would be impressed by him, and that, along with his outward authority, the way would also be paved for her to believe.

One of the powerful jinn offered that he would bring this throne before the gathering ends, as is mentioned in the narrations. Sulayman (peace be upon him) would sit from morning until midday to carry out administrative and judicial decisions. Sulayman (peace be upon him) considered this period to be long, and said that by then it would be too late. So a person who had ﴿knowledge of the Book﴾ (82:03), ﴿the one who had knowledge of the Book﴾, said that he would bring it before the blink of an eye. The Qur'an does not name this person, nor does it mention the Book of which he had knowledge. We believe that he was a believing person, who had a connection with Allah, a man who had attained nearness to God, and that Allah had given him powers for which the veils of the unseen and distances are removed. These are matters and miracles (karamat) whose occurrence sometimes comes from those who have attained nearness to God, and whose secrets are not known to ordinary people, because the world in which ordinary people live, and the means under which they live their lives, are different from this. I think that, to avoid stories, legends and superstitions, at this point only this much can be said.

Some commentators have insisted on who this person was and which Book it was. Regarding the Book, some said it was the Torah, and some said that this person knew the ism a'zam (the greatest name of God), and other commentators have adopted other views. No authentic proof stands behind any of these views. If one adopts a realistic approach, this matter is very simple. There are thousands of secrets of this universe that we do not know. There are countless powers that we have not yet been able to put to use. Within the human soul itself there are secrets to which we have not yet gained access. When Allah makes a person aware of these secrets, then a miracle proceeds for others, because this miracle is hidden from the natural life of ordinary people, while this extraordinary miracle also accords with some power of Allah's own powers, and Allah makes this extraordinary matter happen through whichever hand He wills. (In this way it becomes a miracle and a karamat.)

This person who had knowledge of the Book, because of that knowledge his soul was prepared for this task. Allah had revealed some cosmic secrets to this person, and thus this karamat appeared through his hand, because by virtue of the knowledge of the Book this person had attained nearness to God, and spiritually he was ready for some secrets to be opened to him.

Some commentators said this person was Sulayman (peace be upon him) himself. I think this person was not Sulayman. Otherwise, what was the need to conceal himself? The story was about him, and it was not a story in which his name would need to be kept hidden. Some have said that his name was Asif ibn Barkhiya. There is no proof for this.

The sudden and swift arrival of the throne had a profound effect on Sulayman (peace be upon him). He was frightened that Allah had fulfilled his purpose in such a miraculous manner. He concluded that this was a great blessing from Allah, and His favour and bounty, and that such great generosity is in reality a great trial, a frightening trial. Therefore, he could pass through this trial successfully only if he remained alert at all times, and in this test too, he needed Allah's help for success. He needed the fear of God, it was necessary to be conscious of the blessing, and it was necessary to express gratitude for this favour of Allah, so that it would become evident to Allah that I am grateful, while Allah has no need of anyone's gratitude. Whoever expresses gratitude does so for his own sake, and through gratitude more blessing is attained, and success is achieved in the trial of blessing. And if someone does not express gratitude, and is ungrateful, then Allah is Free of need from the worlds and their inhabitants. He is Generous, and bestows upon those who are grateful without any need.

After making gratitude for blessing, and gratitude itself, a trial, Sulayman prepares to confront the Queen with an astonishing situation.

﴿And [that which] she used to worship besides Allah had kept her away; indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾ (34)

Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him) had prepared another unexpected test to overawe the queen. This test is so sudden that, even at the time of relating the story here, there is no indication of it. Regarding the throne earlier, Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him) had told her that the throne had been brought in a miraculous manner. Here, the style of the Qur'an's expression is also extremely eloquent.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 27, verse 44:

"It was said to her, 'Enter the palace.'" ... "the Lord of the worlds" (34)

This unexpected test was as follows: Solomon had built a magnificent palace. It was a palace of glass. Water had been made to flow beneath its floor, and the floor was of glass, so that the floor appeared like a wave of water. When the queen was told to enter this palace, she thought she had to wade through water. On this she lifted the hems of her trousers, and her legs were exposed. After this incident, Solomon informed her.

"He said: It is a palace paved smooth with glass" (27:44). "She said: 'It is a smooth floor of glass,'" Here the queen was astonished that Solomon possessed amazing wonders, and that these powers were certainly supernatural. Thus she turned towards Allah, and cried out to Allah that the worship of other than Allah which she had performed before had been an injustice to her own soul. Accordingly, together with Solomon (peace be upon him), she declared her acceptance of Islam, saying that she now accepted, along with Solomon, obedience to Allah, the Lord of the worlds.

She had understood what the Islamic system of life is: that in it no human being bows before another human being, but all human beings bow before Allah. Although Solomon is a prophet, she says that she accepts obedience to the Lord of the worlds along with Solomon, meaning that there is companionship with Solomon, just as a Muslim is a companion of other Muslims, but obedience is owed to the Lord of the worlds.

"I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of the worlds" (27:44). The Qur'an has specifically recorded here the point that Islam is for Allah, and by accepting Islam a person stands in a row that is sovereign; indeed, in Islam the powerful and the powerless, and the praised and the lowly, stand in one row. They are brothers; there is no dominant or subordinate. All bow equally before the Lord of the worlds.

The Quraysh adopted arrogance against Islam, although the Messenger of Allah called them to Islam and to obedience to the Lord of the worlds. There is no need to obey Muhammad ibn Abdullah so that he might become a head of state. The Queen of Sheba teaches the Quraysh that accepting the call of a prophet means that a person, in the company of that prophet, becomes obedient to Allah, the Lord of the worlds. The caller and the one called become equal. If they accept Islam, they will be obedient to the Lord of the worlds along with the Messenger of Allah.

**Lesson No. 371: Explanation of Verses 54 to 35**

﴿And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih...﴾ ... ﴿...they [were] disputing﴾ (54)

The story of Prophet Salih and the people of Thamud generally appears in the Qur'an alongside the stories of Prophet Nuh, Prophet Hud, Prophet Lut and Prophet Shu'ayb (peace be upon them). Sometimes the story of Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him) appears with these stories, and sometimes it does not. In this Surah the stories of the Children of Israel also appear. The stories of Prophet Musa, Prophet Dawud and Prophet Sulayman have already passed.

Here too the story of Prophet Hud and Prophet Shu'ayb is mentioned briefly, whereas the story of Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is not mentioned.

In the story of Prophet Salih there is no part about the she-camel. Instead, there is mention of nine *mufsidin* (corrupters) who used to plot against Prophet Salih. Prophet Salih was not aware of their deceptions. In response to their plots, Allah adopted a plan against them which they could not even imagine: He destroyed all those corrupters completely and gave deliverance to Prophet Salih and the believers. The polytheists of Makkah are told: you see their dwellings with your own eyes, yet you do not take a lesson.

﴿And We certainly ... they [were] disputing﴾ (54)

The essence of the mission of Prophet Salih is simply this: "Worship Allah alone." The guidance sent from heaven to mankind in every age has essentially been this same message: worship Allah alone. Every Messenger and every people was taught this. Moreover, in this universe, the signs that surround human beings, and also within human souls themselves, contain intuitive proofs which point to this very truth: the Lord of this universe is One. Yet man denies this simple truth. Not only does he deny it, he also mocks this call and rejects it with contempt, and to this day mankind wanders. He walks along different paths and stumbles, but he does not come to the Straight Path.

Here the Qur'an has mentioned only this effect of the call of Prophet Salih: the people were divided into two groups, and hostility began between them. One group accepted the call, and the other became opposed. The group [that opposed] was much larger in number, as is evident from other Surahs of the Qur'an.

Here, due to the brevity of the story, there is a gap. In it, the people demanded from Prophet Salih: "Bring the punishment with which you threaten us." It is always the method of deniers to demand the punishment of Allah instead of seeking guidance and mercy, just as the polytheists of Quraysh used to demand [this] from the Prophet (ﷺ). Prophet Salih admonished them: what has happened to you, that instead of seeking mercy and guidance you seek the punishment of God? He advises them: seek forgiveness from Allah, and He will have mercy upon you.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 27, verse 46:**

Qala ya qawmi lima ... tarhamun (64)

The minds of people have become so corrupted that those who deny the truth began to say: "O Allah, if this man is Your messenger and is upon the truth, then rain down stones upon us and send down a painful punishment." Yet they should have said: "O Allah, if this man has come from You and is truthful, then grant us the ability to believe and to affirm him."

The same was the condition of the people of Salih. Their messenger calls them to the path of mercy, repentance and seeking forgiveness, and instead of accepting this call, these people declare: "We have become fed up with Salih and with those who have joined him, for these people have become a calamity for us, and we fear that they will bring some great misfortune upon us."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (*Fi Zilal al-Quran*, Urdu translation) on Surah 27, verse 47:

﴿They said, "We consider you and those with you to be a bad omen."﴾

*Tatayyur* (bad omen, augury) means taking omens of ill fortune. This word comes from the superstitions and fables of ignorant peoples. These are the illusions from which a person can escape only through pure and straightforward faith. In the days of *Jahiliyyah* (the age of ignorance, before Islam), if someone intended to set out for some task, he would seek a good or bad omen from a bird. He would scare a bird that was sitting in some place. If the bird flew from his right side to his left, he would be pleased and carry out the task. But if the bird flew from his left side to his right, he would take it as a bad omen and consider the matter dangerous. The question is: how can anyone know where a bird should go and where it should not? Moreover, how can unseen matters be known from the accidental movement of a bird? The truth is that the human self always hands over its affairs to some unseen power. Lesson No. 175: At a Glance

This passage concludes Surah al-Naml. Within it, brief episodes from the lives of Musa, Dawud, Sulayman, Salih and Lut (peace be upon them) have been brought in. This conclusion is in harmony with the beginning of the surah. Likewise, it is linked with the surah's theme and subject matter. Each story establishes the purpose that the surah has in view.

This lesson begins with the praise of Allah, and peace is sent upon those servants of Allah who are chosen. Among them are the prophets and messengers whose stories have been related in this surah. After this praise and salutation, the exposition of the Islamic worldview and Islamic belief begins again. In it are described the proofs of Tawhid from this universe, the intuitive proofs found within the human self, certain unseen matters and the signs of the Last Day, and then the witnessing of the Last Day, and then the terrifying moments of the gathering and scattering (resurrection). In those moments, all creatures of the heavens and the earth will be terrified, except the one whom Allah saves.

In this lesson, human beings are shown certain observations of the human self and of this universe. No person can deny these observations and these proofs. And no one can give any explanation of them except this: that there exists one single Creator Being, who is supremely wise in governance and possessed of power.

These observations come in continuous and highly effective blows, they establish proof against a person and awaken his consciousness. There are continuous questions, whose true answer is only this: who is Allah? Who created the heavens and the earth? Who sent down water from the sky by which We caused lush gardens to grow? Who holds the earth steady? Who made rivers flow within the earth? Who set up towering mountains on the earth? Who set barriers between two rivers and seas? Who hears the call of one in distress and removes his suffering? Who makes you vicegerents on the earth, granting you authority within it? Who guides you in the darkness of land and sea? Then who sends the cool wind before His mercy (rain)? Who originates creation and then will repeat it? Who provides you sustenance from the sky and the earth? These questions come continuously, and after every question they are shaken again: is there any god besides Allah? Therefore no reasonable person can claim that there is another god along with Allah. No one can make such a claim. Yet, despite this, their conduct is that they worship other deities besides Allah.

These blows strike directly upon the human heart, because these are the pages of the open book of this universe, and this is their conscious intuition which they perceive. Yet these people still deny the Hereafter, and in matters of the Hereafter they are subject to extreme confusion. They are therefore alerted that earlier nations also denied in the same way, and Allah destroyed them. Here the discourse again returns to the terrifying scenes of the gathering and scattering. Observe how, in every moment, the readers are again brought back into the world, and the scenes of the Day of Resurrection come again in a most frightening manner. Thus human hearts are shaken and thoroughly jolted.

At the end of this lesson, a decisive blow is delivered, like one who makes a final statement, warns of dreadful consequences, gives a last warning, and then rises and departs. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ is told to leave these mockers and deniers of the Hereafter to their own state. You (ﷺ) have directed them to the cosmic proofs; you have also presented the terrifying scenes of the Day of Judgment. So now let them be left, so that they may reach their natural end, because they themselves have chosen that end for themselves. They are told that the duty of the Messenger ﷺ is limited and defined, and the means available to the Messenger are limited, because after warning, the choice is theirs, whether they adopt the right path or not.
